// instead of inlining the full shape at every call site. The prefix is
// the namespace's camelCased name, capitalised (`Sheets_Spreadsheet`,
// `Drive_File`) so two realms that both define `File` don't collide.

export interface WorldTools {
  agLobbyists: {
    /** One lobbying firm's full register record — ABN, dates, lobbyists with former-government- representative declarations, clients and stakeholders. */
    organisationProfile(args: { id: string }): Promise<{ summary?: { id?: string; displayName?: string; tradingName?: string; abn?: string; registeredOn?: string; modifiedOn?: string; dateDeregistered?: string | null; isDeregistered?: boolean }; lobbyists?: Array<{ displayName?: string; position?: string; isFormerRepresentative?: boolean; previousPosition?: string | null; previousPositionOther?: string | null; cessationDate?: string | null; datePublished?: string }>; clients?: Array<Record<string, unknown>>; stakeholders?: Array<{ lastName?: string | null; businessName?: string | null; isBusiness?: boolean }> }>;

    /** The whole register as a typeahead index — every organisation, lobbyist and client entry, each row carrying the owning organisation's GUID. ~720KB, one call, no paging. */
    registerIndex(args: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<{ categories?: Array<string>; data?: Array<{ category?: string; displayName?: string; description?: string; descriptionCaption?: string; organisationId?: string }> }>;
  };
  ai: {
    /** Classify each item in a list against an instruction. `items` is an ARRAY of strings — pass it directly (e.g. `rows.map(r => r.what)`), do NOT JSON.stringify. `categories` is an optional comma-separated set of allowed labels (omit for a free label or yes/no). Returns a JSON array of {index, category, reason} in input order. Use this to apply a fuzzy predicate the graph can't express — "which of these sound urgent", "what kind of expense is each" — over rows from the KG, without a second turn. `role` is OPTIONAL — omit it for the world default, or pass one of 'cheap' | 'workhorse' | 'best' to pick a model tier. */
    classify(args: { instruction: string; items: unknown[]; categories?: string; role?: string }): Promise<Array<{ index: number; category: string; reason: string }>>;

    /** Run a single free-form LLM prompt and return the model's text. Use this to apply judgement to data you already have — build a prompt that lists rows (e.g. from the knowledge graph) and asks for a per-row verdict or a short summary. Returns the raw completion as a string; you parse it. Side-effect free. `role` is OPTIONAL — omit it for the world default, or pass one of 'cheap' | 'workhorse' | 'best' to pick a model tier. */
    complete(args: { prompt: string; role?: string }): Promise<string>;
  };
  artifacts: {
    /** Delete a world artifact. */
    deleteArtifact(args: { type: string; name: string }): Promise<unknown>;

    /** List all world artifacts by type (apps, code, datasets, diagrams). */
    listArtifacts(args: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<unknown>;

    /** Read the content of a world artifact. */
    readArtifact(args: { type: string; name: string }): Promise<unknown>;

    /** Create or update a world artifact (diagrams, code, datasets). For diagrams use type=DIAGRAM with a `.mmd` filename and Mermaid source — after writing, the diagram is rendered at `/diagrams/{filename}` and you should share that link with the user. Do NOT use for HTML apps — those are built with the dedicated app-building tool, not this one. */
    writeArtifact(args: { type: string; name: string; content: string }): Promise<unknown>;
  };
  arxiv: {
    /** Search arXiv papers. Call: searchArxiv({ search_query: 'all:graph memory agent', max_results: 5 }). Returns an Atom XML feed.. Search arXiv for papers, or fetch specific papers by id. Pass EITHER `search_query` (a search) OR `id_list` (exact arXiv ids).  search_query syntax — combine field-prefixed terms with AND / OR / ANDNOT:   all: (any field)   ti: (title)    au: (author)   abs: (abstract)    cat: (category, e.g. cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML) Quote multi-word phrases. Examples:   all:graph-based memory for agents   ti:"retrieval augmented generation" AND cat:cs.CL   au:hinton AND abs:capsule NOTE: bare spaces are treated as OR between terms, so for an AND/phrase query be explicit (use AND, or quote the phrase).  RESPONSE IS ATOM XML, not JSON. Read each <entry>:   <title>            — paper title   <summary>          — abstract   <author><name>     — one per author   <published>        — first submission date (ISO-8601)   <updated>          — last revision date   <id>               — the abstract page URL (http://arxiv.org/abs/ID); cite THIS   <link title="pdf"> — the PDF URL (href attribute)   <category term=>   — subject categories; arxiv:primary_category is the main one <opensearch:totalResults> gives the total match count (only max_results are returned).  Cite the <id> (abs page) URL for each paper you reference. */
    searchArxiv(args: { search_query?: string; id_list?: string; start?: number; max_results?: number; sortBy?: string; sortOrder?: string }): Promise<string>;
  };
  assert: {
    /** Assert entities into the knowledge graph. Each entity is resolved against existing data — matching entities are updated, new ones are created. Provide a list of entities with name, labels (types like Person, Company), optional description, and optional properties. */
    entities(args: { entities: unknown[] }): Promise<unknown>;

    /** Assert entities and relationships into the knowledge graph. Entities are resolved first (matched or created), then relationships are created between them. Relationship source and target must match entity names from the entities list. */
    entitiesAndRelationships(args: { entities: unknown[]; relationships: unknown[] }): Promise<unknown>;
  };
  assess: {
    /** Look at an image the user has — a figure/diagram/chart from a document, or an image they uploaded in chat — and answer a SPECIFIC visual question about it: count elements, compare bars, read a value or label off the image. Use when the indexed description doesn't contain the detail asked for. The figureId appears on figure/image chunks in search results. */
    figure(args: { figureId: string; question: string }): Promise<unknown>;
  };
  attachment: {
    /** Read the FIRST FEW HUNDRED characters of an attachment the user shared, to check whether it is a format you handle. Use this when deciding whether to claim a file — it is cheap, and reading a whole file to look at its first line is not. Returns the prefix as text, or an error if the attachment is not yours or is gone. Use `attachment_read` once you have decided to act on it. */
    head(args: { storageKey: string; maxChars?: number }): Promise<unknown>;

    /** List files the user has attached, most recent first. Use this FIRST when the user refers to a file they shared — "this file", "the export I just sent", or a filename — because reading one requires its storageKey and this is the only way to learn it. Returns filename, when it arrived, and the storageKey to pass to `attachment_head` or `attachment_read`. NEVER ask the user to upload a file again because you cannot find it: check here first. */
    list(args: { limit?: number }): Promise<unknown>;

    /** Read the FULL text content of an attachment the user shared, so you can parse it. Use this only after deciding to act on the file — check the format with `attachment_head` first. Returns the content as text, or an error if the attachment is not yours, is gone, or is too large to read as text. */
    read(args: { storageKey: string; force?: boolean }): Promise<unknown>;
  };
  austender: {
    /** Every published version of one contract notice — the original release plus one release per amendment, each with the value as amended. The base CN id (e.g. CN3942784) returns the whole chain; asking for an amendment id (CN3942784-A1) returns no records. */
    findContractNoticeById(args: { cnid: string }): Promise<Austender_ReleasePackage>;

    /** Releases LAST MODIFIED in the window — this is where amendment releases surface (tag `contractAmendment`), alongside newly published notices. The feed for "what changed", as distinct from "what was signed". */
    findContractsModifiedBetween(args: { from: string; to: string; cursor?: string }): Promise<Austender_ReleasePackage>;

    /** Contract notices FIRST PUBLISHED in the window, NEWEST FIRST (measured live 2026-08-01 — a capped walk covers the window's most recent days, not its start), 100 per page. ISO instants, e.g. 2026-07-01T00:00:00Z. New contracts only — amendments to older contracts do not appear here; use findContractsModifiedBetween for change-shaped questions. */
    findContractsPublishedBetween(args: { from: string; to: string; cursor?: string }): Promise<Austender_ReleasePackage>;
  };
  brave: {
    /** Search news articles with Brave. Call: newsSearch({ q: '...', count: 5 }). The query field is named `q`, not `query`.. Returns news articles for the query. Use when the user explicitly wants news / headlines / current events. For general knowledge prefer webSearch. The query string MUST be passed as `q` (single letter). */
    newsSearch(args: { q: string; count?: number; country?: string; freshness?: string }): Promise<Brave_NewsSearchResponse>;

    /** Search the web with Brave. Call: webSearch({ q: '...', count: 5 }). The query field is named `q`, not `query`.. Returns web pages relevant to the query. Use for general web information, current facts, "what is" / "who is" lookups, product / company background, and any topic where stale training data is a risk. The query string MUST be passed as `q` (single letter) — `query` will produce HTTP 422 missing-q. */
    webSearch(args: { q: string; count?: number; offset?: number; country?: string; freshness?: string }): Promise<Brave_WebSearchResponse>;
  };
  cypher: {
    /** Same read-only virtual-cypher engine and per-user scope as `kg_query`, BUT it takes NO `params` — so for any query with a user-supplied or variable value, use `kg_query` (`gateway.kg.query({ cypher, params })`) and bind it; never interpolate a value into this `cypher` string. This `gateway.cypher.query` alias is for fixed, literal queries in `code_mode` scripts. Runs a read-only Cypher query (per-user scoped; on-demand virtual joins materialize). Returns {"rows": [...], "warnings": [...]}: rows are row objects keyed by your RETURN aliases, and a node column carries its type under `__type` so results can be hydrated to typed instances. warnings is usually empty; when non-empty a backing source failed or truncated, so few/zero rows means "source unavailable", not "no data". A query using relationships or shapes the schema does not contain FAILS with the relevant schema in the error — correct the query from it and call again. */
    query(args: { cypher: string }): Promise<{ rows: Array<Record<string, unknown>>; warnings: Array<string>; freshness?: Array<{ producer?: string; source?: string; observedAt?: string; keys?: number }>; hint?: string; cost?: { ms?: number; apiCalls?: number; llmCalls?: number } }>;
  };
  dataGovAu: {
    /** Full-text search over the catalogue. Returns matching datasets NEWEST-METADATA-FIRST by relevance, each with its resources (the downloadable files) inline — id, URL, format and size per resource. A dated-extract series (one dataset per extract) comes back as one row per extract, so the dataset TITLES carry the series' timeline. */
    searchDatasets(args: { q: string; rows?: number }): Promise<{ success?: boolean; result?: { count?: number; results?: Array<{ id?: string; title?: string; metadata_modified?: string; license_id?: string; organization?: { title?: string }; resources?: Array<{ id?: string; name?: string; url?: string; format?: string; size?: number; last_modified?: string }> }> } }>;
  };
  do: {
    /** Run one verb on the user's own computer through their Embabel Me app. Use the exact verb name and argument names from list_host_verbs — call that first if you have not this turn. Anything the machine does not offer is refused by the machine, not attempted. */
    hostVerb(args: { args: Record<string, unknown>; verb: string }): Promise<unknown>;
  };
  email: {
    /** Vector (semantic) search over the user's recent email-thread summaries. Pass a topic or question (a meeting subject, a person + theme, or e.g. 'capital call wire instructions'); returns matching threads' summary text with a relevance score. Use to pull relevant past context an exact participant or keyword match would miss. */
    search(args: { query: string; topK?: number }): Promise<Array<{ summary: string; score: number }>>;
  };
  emailThreads: {
    /** given a chunk ID, expand to surrounding chunks */
    broadenChunk(args: { chunkId: string; chunksToAdd?: number }): Promise<string>;

    /** Fetch a single email thread by its threadId — use this after vectorSearch / textSearch surfaces an interesting summary to read the actual conversation. Pass the threadId from the summary's metadata (typically a hex-ish string). Returns subject + participants + per-message bodies, or an error message if the thread isn't in the store. */
    getEmailThread(args: { threadId: string }): Promise<string>;

    /** Perform BM25 text search. Specify topK and similarity threshold from 0-1.  Query syntax: Plain text — type the user's question as they said it. Punctuation, URLs, file paths and code fragments are all safe: they are searched for, not interpreted, so nothing you write can fail to parse. Query operators are NOT available and will be matched literally if typed. Identifiers in the question — error codes, part numbers, ticket references — are matched exactly on your behalf, so you do not need to mark them. */
    textSearch(args: { query: string; topK: number; threshold?: number }): Promise<string>;

    /** Perform vector search. Specify topK. Ranking handles relevance — omit threshold unless you have a specific reason to floor it. */
    vectorSearch(args: { query: string; topK: number; threshold?: number }): Promise<string>;

    /** given a content element ID, expand to parent section. If the result is too large, use vectorSearch or textSearch with a more specific query instead. */
    zoomOut(args: { id: string }): Promise<string>;
  };
  fetch: {
    /** Fetch a page AND a bounded selection of its most relevant same-site links in ONE call, returning every page's readable text. Use when a landing page is a shell ('click to explore') or the user asks what's on a site. Prefer plain fetch for a single known URL. */
    crawl(args: { url: string; hint?: string; max_pages?: number }): Promise<unknown>;

    /** Fetch a URL and return its readable text content (HTML is reduced to titled sections; PDF and other document formats are extracted too), followed by the page's links. If the page itself is thin, its substance is behind those links — fetch them to explore the site. Long pages are truncated — re-call with start_index to page through. */
    fetch(args: { url: string; max_length?: number; start_index?: number }): Promise<unknown>;
  };
  find: {
    /** Look up an entity (person, organization, biller, SaaS service, email domain, …) by name. Try this FIRST for "who is X" / "what is X" / "do I know X". On an empty array: if the name could be a concept, term, or topic from the user's documents (a spec/report/framework term, a body defined in a document), search the document tools (`reference_docs`) NEXT, in the SAME turn — do NOT ask permission or offer to search, just search. Only fall back to external tools (a connected integration, web) after that, and never report "no information" before the document search.  Returns Array<EntityHit> (id, name, label, description, `fields`). `fields` carries a single-hop edge rollup (`worksFor`, `livesIn`, …) that answers simple one-relationship questions directly. This is a SUMMARY, not the full answer — for drilldown / aggregate / join / top-N (e.g. "her other email addresses", "everyone who works there"), ask `ask_kg` in plain English, or pass the `id` into `kg_neighbors` to walk its edges; don't stop at the summary, and don't fall back to email-thread search for an entity's attributes. Empty array = no match. Resolved hits are pinned to the session. */
    entity(args: { name: string; type?: string }): Promise<Array<{ id: string; name: string; label: string; description?: string; fields: Record<string, string> }>>;

    /** Fetch ONE entity by its id — the exact `id` value from `find_entity` or a `kg_query` row — as the full typed object: its properties plus a one-hop neighbourhood rollup. Use this once you've LOCATED an entity (by name or query) and need its details, instead of re-querying. In code-mode the returned object is TYPED, so you can call its methods, not just read fields. (Named for Spring's findById; pairs with `find_entity`, which looks up by name.) */
    entityById(args: { entityId: string }): Promise<{ id: string; name: string; labels: Array<string>; properties: Record<string, string>; outgoing?: Array<{ edge?: string; edgeProps?: Record<string, string>; to?: { id?: string; name?: string; labels?: Array<string> } }>; incoming?: Array<{ edge?: string; edgeProps?: Record<string, string>; from?: { id?: string; name?: string; labels?: Array<string> } }>; samples?: Array<{ neighbourId?: string; neighbourName?: string; snippet?: string }> }>;
  };

    /** Get a pull request. Draft pull requests are available in public repositories with GitHub Free and GitHub Free for organizations, GitHub Pro, and legacy per-repository billing plans, and in public and private repositories with GitHub Team and GitHub Enterprise Cloud. For more information, see [GitHub's products](https://docs.github.com/github/getting-started-with-github/githubs-products) in the GitHub Help documentation.  Lists details of a pull request by providing its number.  When you get, [create](https://docs.github.com/rest/pulls/pulls/#create-a-pull-request), or [edit](https://docs.github.com/rest/pulls/pulls#update-a-pull-request) a pull request, GitHub creates a merge commit to test whether the pull request can be automatically merged into the base branch. This test commit is not added to the base branch or the head branch. You can review the status of the test commit using the `mergeable` key. For more information, see "[Checking mergeability of pull requests](https://docs.github.com/rest/guides/getting-started-with-the-git-database-api#checking-mergeability-of-pull-requests)".  The value of the `mergeable` attribute can be `true`, `false`, or `null`. If the value is `null`, then GitHub has started a background job to compute the mergeability. After giving the job time to complete, resubmit the request. When the job finishes, you will see a non-`null` value for the `mergeable` attribute in the response. If `mergeable` is `true`, then `merge_commit_sha` will be the SHA of the _test_ merge commit.  The value of the `merge_commit_sha` attribute changes depending on the state of the pull request. Before merging a pull request, the `merge_commit_sha` attribute holds the SHA of the _test_ merge commit. After merging a pull request, the `merge_commit_sha` attribute changes depending on how you merged the pull request:  *   If merged as a [merge commit](https://docs.github.com/articles/about-merge-methods-on-github/), `merge_commit_sha` represents the SHA of the merge commit. *   If merged via a [squash](https://docs.github.com/articles/about-merge-methods-on-github/#squashing-your-merge-commits), `merge_commit_sha` represents the SHA of the squashed commit on the base branch. *   If [rebased](https://docs.github.com/articles/about-merge-methods-on-github/#rebasing-and-merging-your-commits), `merge_commit_sha` represents the commit that the base branch was updated to.  Pass the appropriate [media type](https://docs.github.com/rest/using-the-rest-api/getting-started-with-the-rest-api#media-types) to fetch diff and patch formats.  This endpoint supports the following custom media types. For more information, see "[Media types](https://docs.github.com/rest/using-the-rest-api/getting-started-with-the-rest-api#media-types)."  - **`application/vnd.github.raw+json`**: Returns the raw markdown body. Response will include `body`. This is the default if you do not pass any specific media type. - **`application/vnd.github.text+json`**: Returns a text only representation of the markdown body. Response will include `body_text`. - **`application/vnd.github.html+json`**: Returns HTML rendered from the body's markdown. Response will include `body_html`. - **`application/vnd.github.full+json`**: Returns raw, text, and HTML representations. Response will include `body`, `body_text`, and `body_html`. - **`application/vnd.github.diff`**: For more information, see "[git-diff](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-diff)" in the Git documentation. If a diff is corrupt, contact us through the [GitHub Support portal](https://support.github.com/). Include the repository name and pull request ID in your message. */
    pullsGet(args: { owner: string; repo: string; pull_number: number }): Promise<Gh_PullRequest>;

    reposGet(args: { owner: string; repo: string }): Promise<Gh_FullRepository>;

    /** Get repository content. Gets the contents of a file or directory in a repository. Specify the file path or directory with the `path` parameter. If you omit the `path` parameter, you will receive the contents of the repository's root directory.  This endpoint supports the following custom media types. For more information, see "[Media types](https://docs.github.com/rest/using-the-rest-api/getting-started-with-the-rest-api#media-types)."  - **`application/vnd.github.raw+json`**: Returns the raw file contents for files and symlinks. - **`application/vnd.github.html+json`**: Returns the file contents in HTML. Markup languages are rendered to HTML using GitHub's open-source [Markup library](https://github.com/github/markup). - **`application/vnd.github.object+json`**: Returns the contents in a consistent object format regardless of the content type. For example, instead of an array of objects for a directory, the response will be an object with an `entries` attribute containing the array of objects.  If the content is a directory, the response will be an array of objects, one object for each item in the directory. When listing the contents of a directory, submodules have their "type" specified as "file". Logically, the value _should_ be "submodule". This behavior exists [for backwards compatibility purposes](https://git.io/v1YCW). In the next major version of the API, the type will be returned as "submodule".  If the content is a symlink and the symlink's target is a normal file in the repository, then the API responds with the content of the file. Otherwise, the API responds with an object describing the symlink itself.  If the content is a submodule, the `submodule_git_url` field identifies the location of the submodule repository, and the `sha` identifies a specific commit within the submodule repository. Git uses the given URL when cloning the submodule repository, and checks out the submodule at that specific commit. If the submodule repository is not hosted on github.com, the Git URLs (`git_url` and `_links["git"]`) and the github.com URLs (`html_url` and `_links["html"]`) will have null values.  **Notes**:  - To get a repository's contents recursively, you can [recursively get the tree](https://docs.github.com/rest/git/trees#get-a-tree). - This API has an upper limit of 1,000 files for a directory. If you need to retrieve more files, use the [Git Trees API](https://docs.github.com/rest/git/trees#get-a-tree). - Download URLs expire and are meant to be used just once. To ensure the download URL does not expire, please use the contents API to obtain a fresh download URL for each download. - If the requested file's size is:   - 1 MB or smaller: All features of this endpoint are supported.   - Between 1-100 MB: Only the `raw` or `object` custom media types are supported. Both will work as normal, except that when using the `object` media type, the `content` field will be an empty string and the `encoding` field will be `"none"`. To get the contents of these larger files, use the `raw` media type.   - Greater than 100 MB: This endpoint is not supported. */
    reposGetContent(args: { owner: string; repo: string; path: string; ref?: string }): Promise<Gh_ContentDirectory | Gh_ContentFile | Gh_ContentSymlink | Gh_ContentSubmodule>;

    /** Get the latest release. View the latest published full release for the repository.  The latest release is the most recent non-prerelease, non-draft release, sorted by the `created_at` attribute. The `created_at` attribute is the date of the commit used for the release, and not the date when the release was drafted or published. */
    reposGetLatestRelease(args: { owner: string; repo: string }): Promise<Gh_Release>;

    /** Get a repository README. Gets the preferred README for a repository.  This endpoint supports the following custom media types. For more information, see "[Media types](https://docs.github.com/rest/using-the-rest-api/getting-started-with-the-rest-api#media-types)."  - **`application/vnd.github.raw+json`**: Returns the raw file contents. This is the default if you do not specify a media type. - **`application/vnd.github.html+json`**: Returns the README in HTML. Markup languages are rendered to HTML using GitHub's open-source [Markup library](https://github.com/github/markup). */
    reposGetReadme(args: { owner: string; repo: string; ref?: string }): Promise<Gh_ContentFile>;

    /** List branches. */
    reposListBranches(args: { owner: string; repo: string; protected?: boolean; per_page?: number; page?: number }): Promise<Array<Gh_ShortBranch>>;

    /** List commits. **Signature verification object**  The response will include a `verification` object that describes the result of verifying the commit's signature. The following fields are included in the `verification` object:  | Name | Type | Description | | ---- | ---- | ----------- | | `verified` | `boolean` | Indicates whether GitHub considers the signature in this commit to be verified. | | `reason` | `string` | The reason for verified value. Possible values and their meanings are enumerated in table below. | | `signature` | `string` | The signature that was extracted from the commit. | | `payload` | `string` | The value that was signed. | | `verified_at` | `string` | The date the signature was verified by GitHub. |  These are the possible values for `reason` in the `verification` object:  | Value | Description | | ----- | ----------- | | `expired_key` | The key that made the signature is expired. | | `not_signing_key` | The "signing" flag is not among the usage flags in the GPG key that made the signature. | | `gpgverify_error` | There was an error communicating with the signature verification service. | | `gpgverify_unavailable` | The signature verification service is currently unavailable. | | `unsigned` | The object does not include a signature. | | `unknown_signature_type` | A non-PGP signature was found in the commit. | | `no_user` | No user was associated with the `committer` email address in the commit. | | `unverified_email` | The `committer` email address in the commit was associated with a user, but the email address is not verified on their account. | | `bad_email` | The `committer` email address in the commit is not included in the identities of the PGP key that made the signature. | | `unknown_key` | The key that made the signature has not been registered with any user's account. | | `malformed_signature` | There was an error parsing the signature. | | `invalid` | The signature could not be cryptographically verified using the key whose key-id was found in the signature. | | `valid` | None of the above errors applied, so the signature is considered to be verified. | */
    reposListCommits(args: { owner: string; repo: string; sha?: string; path?: string; author?: string; committer?: string; since?: string; until?: string; per_page?: number; page?: number }): Promise<Array<Gh_Commit>>;

    /** List repository contributors. Lists contributors to the specified repository and sorts them by the number of commits per contributor in descending order. This endpoint may return information that is a few hours old because the GitHub REST API caches contributor data to improve performance.  GitHub identifies contributors by author email address. This endpoint groups contribution counts by GitHub user, which includes all associated email addresses. To improve performance, only the first 500 author email addresses in the repository link to GitHub users. The rest will appear as anonymous contributors without associated GitHub user information. */
    reposListContributors(args: { owner: string; repo: string; anon?: string; per_page?: number; page?: number }): Promise<Array<Gh_Contributor>>;

    /** List repositories for the authenticated user. Lists repositories that the authenticated user has explicit permission (`:read`, `:write`, or `:admin`) to access.  The authenticated user has explicit permission to access repositories they own, repositories where they are a collaborator, and repositories that they can access through an organization membership. */
    reposListForAuthenticatedUser(args: { visibility?: string; affiliation?: string; type?: string; sort?: string; direction?: string; per_page?: number; page?: number; since?: string; before?: string }): Promise<Array<Gh_Repository>>;

    /** List repositories for a user. Lists public repositories for the specified user. */
    reposListForUser(args: { username: string; type?: string; sort?: string; direction?: string; per_page?: number; page?: number }): Promise<Array<Gh_MinimalRepository>>;

    /** List releases. This returns a list of releases, which does not include regular Git tags that have not been associated with a release. To get a list of Git tags, use the [Repository Tags API](https://docs.github.com/rest/repos/repos#list-repository-tags).  Information about published releases are available to everyone. Only users with push access will receive listings for draft releases. */
    reposListReleases(args: { owner: string; repo: string; per_page?: number; page?: number }): Promise<Array<Gh_Release>>;

    /** List repository tags. */
    reposListTags(args: { owner: string; repo: string; per_page?: number; page?: number }): Promise<Array<Gh_Tag>>;

    /** Search code. Searches for query terms inside of a file. This method returns up to 100 results [per page](https://docs.github.com/rest/guides/using-pagination-in-the-rest-api).  When searching for code, you can get text match metadata for the file **content** and file **path** fields when you pass the `text-match` media type. For more details about how to receive highlighted search results, see [Text match metadata](https://docs.github.com/rest/search/search#text-match-metadata).  For example, if you want to find the definition of the `addClass` function inside [jQuery](https://github.com/jquery/jquery) repository, your query would look something like this:  `q=addClass+in:file+language:js+repo:jquery/jquery`  This query searches for the keyword `addClass` within a file's contents. The query limits the search to files where the language is JavaScript in the `jquery/jquery` repository.  Considerations for code search:  Due to the complexity of searching code, there are a few restrictions on how searches are performed:  *   Only the _default branch_ is considered. In most cases, this will be the `master` branch. *   Only files smaller than 384 KB are searchable. *   You must always include at least one search term when searching source code. For example, searching for [`language:go`](https://github.com/search?utf8=%E2%9C%93&q=language%3Ago&type=Code) is not valid, while [`amazing language:go`](https://github.com/search?utf8=%E2%9C%93&q=amazing+language%3Ago&type=Code) is.  > [!NOTE] > `repository.description`, `repository.owner.type`, and `repository.owner.node_id` are closing down on this endpoint and will return `null` in a future API version. Use the [Get a repository](https://docs.github.com/rest/repos/repos#get-a-repository) endpoint (`GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}`) to retrieve full repository metadata.  This endpoint requires you to authenticate and limits you to 10 requests per minute. */
    searchCode(args: { q: string; sort?: string; order?: string; per_page?: number; page?: number }): Promise<{ total_count: number; incomplete_results: boolean; items: Array<Gh_CodeSearchResultItem> }>;

    /** Search issues and pull requests. Find issues by state and keyword. This method returns up to 100 results [per page](https://docs.github.com/rest/guides/using-pagination-in-the-rest-api).  When searching for issues, you can get text match metadata for the issue **title**, issue **body**, and issue **comment body** fields when you pass the `text-match` media type. For more details about how to receive highlighted search results, see [Text match metadata](https://docs.github.com/rest/search/search#text-match-metadata).  For example, if you want to find the oldest unresolved Python bugs on Windows. Your query might look something like this.  `q=windows+label:bug+language:python+state:open&sort=created&order=asc`  This query searches for the keyword `windows`, within any open issue that is labeled as `bug`. The search runs across repositories whose primary language is Python. The results are sorted by creation date in ascending order, which means the oldest issues appear first in the search results.  > [!NOTE] > For requests made by GitHub Apps with a user access token, you can't retrieve a combination of issues and pull requests in a single query. Requests that don't include the `is:issue` or `is:pull-request` qualifier will receive an HTTP `422 Unprocessable Entity` response. To get results for both issues and pull requests, you must send separate queries for issues and pull requests. For more information about the `is` qualifier, see "[Searching only issues or pull requests](https://docs.github.com/github/searching-for-information-on-github/searching-issues-and-pull-requests#search-only-issues-or-pull-requests)." */
    searchIssuesAndPullRequests(args: { q: string; sort?: string; order?: string; per_page?: number; page?: number; advanced_search?: string; search_type?: string }): Promise<{ total_count: number; incomplete_results: boolean; items: Array<Gh_IssueSearchResultItem>; search_type: string; lexical_fallback_reason?: Array<string> }>;

    /** Search repositories. Find repositories via various criteria. This method returns up to 100 results [per page](https://docs.github.com/rest/guides/using-pagination-in-the-rest-api).  When searching for repositories, you can get text match metadata for the **name** and **description** fields when you pass the `text-match` media type. For more details about how to receive highlighted search results, see [Text match metadata](https://docs.github.com/rest/search/search#text-match-metadata).  For example, if you want to search for popular Tetris repositories written in assembly code, your query might look like this:  `q=tetris+language:assembly&sort=stars&order=desc`  This query searches for repositories with the word `tetris` in the name, the description, or the README. The results are limited to repositories where the primary language is assembly. The results are sorted by stars in descending order, so that the most popular repositories appear first in the search results. */
    searchRepos(args: { q: string; sort?: string; order?: string; per_page?: number; page?: number }): Promise<{ total_count: number; incomplete_results: boolean; items: Array<Gh_RepoSearchResultItem> }>;

    /** Search users. Find users via various criteria. This method returns up to 100 results [per page](https://docs.github.com/rest/guides/using-pagination-in-the-rest-api).  When searching for users, you can get text match metadata for the issue **login**, public **email**, and **name** fields when you pass the `text-match` media type. For more details about highlighting search results, see [Text match metadata](https://docs.github.com/rest/search/search#text-match-metadata). For more details about how to receive highlighted search results, see [Text match metadata](https://docs.github.com/rest/search/search#text-match-metadata).  For example, if you're looking for a list of popular users, you might try this query:  `q=tom+repos:%3E42+followers:%3E1000`  This query searches for users with the name `tom`. The results are restricted to users with more than 42 repositories and over 1,000 followers.  This endpoint does not accept authentication and will only include publicly visible users. As an alternative, you can use the GraphQL API. The GraphQL API requires authentication and will return private users, including Enterprise Managed Users (EMUs), that you are authorized to view. For more information, see "[GraphQL Queries](https://docs.github.com/graphql/reference/queries#search)." */
    searchUsers(args: { q: string; sort?: string; order?: string; per_page?: number; page?: number }): Promise<{ total_count: number; incomplete_results: boolean; items: Array<Gh_UserSearchResultItem> }>;

    /** Get the authenticated user. OAuth app tokens and personal access tokens (classic) need the `user` scope in order for the response to include private profile information. */
    usersGetAuthenticated(args: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<Gh_PrivateUser | Gh_PublicUser>;

    /** Get a user. Provides publicly available information about someone with a GitHub account.  If you are requesting information about an [Enterprise Managed User](https://docs.github.com/enterprise-cloud@latest/admin/managing-iam/understanding-iam-for-enterprises/about-enterprise-managed-users), or a GitHub App bot that is installed in an organization that uses Enterprise Managed Users, your requests must be authenticated as a user or GitHub App that has access to the organization to view that account's information. If you are not authorized, the request will return a `404 Not Found` status.  The `email` key in the following response is the publicly visible email address from your GitHub [profile page](https://github.com/settings/profile). When setting up your profile, you can select a primary email address to be public which provides an email entry for this endpoint. If you do not set a public email address for `email`, then it will have a value of `null`. You only see publicly visible email addresses when authenticated with GitHub. For more information, see [Authentication](https://docs.github.com/rest/guides/getting-started-with-the-rest-api#authentication).  The Emails API enables you to list all of your email addresses, and toggle a primary email to be visible publicly. For more information, see [Emails API](https://docs.github.com/rest/users/emails). */
    usersGetByUsername(args: { username: string }): Promise<Gh_PrivateUser | Gh_PublicUser>;
  };
  identity: {
    /** Record that an external identity (a connected account or handle, email             address, …) belongs to a specific person. Use IMMEDIATELY whenever the             user states who a handle or address belongs to — even in passing —             because acknowledging without recording LOSES the correction. Never             model a handle as a person's alias or attribute; it is a linked identity. This is authoritative: automatic matching will             respect it and never contradict it. Look the person up first to get             their graph id; if no such person exists in the user's world yet,             create the person there and then link — do not give up. Do NOT use for             sign-in accounts — those are managed by the sign-in flow itself. */
    link(args: { provider: string; external_id: string; person_id: string; evidence: string }): Promise<unknown>;

    /** Show which external identities (connected accounts, email, …) are linked to             a person, with who asserted each link and why — plus any identities the             user has explicitly said are NOT this person. Use before linking or             unlinking, or when the user asks how someone is connected. */
    list(args: { person_id: string }): Promise<unknown>;

    /** Remove a wrong identity link whenever the user retracts or denies one             ("that's not their handle", "I was wrong about that account") —             acknowledging without removing leaves the wrong link in place. The correction             is remembered permanently: automatic matching will not re-create the             link. Use identity_list first if unsure what is currently linked. */
    unlink(args: { provider: string; external_id: string; person_id: string; reason: string }): Promise<unknown>;
  };
  images: {
    /** Add or update description and tags for an image. Use this after analyzing an image in conversation. */
    annotateImage(args: { filename: string; description: string; tags?: string }): Promise<unknown>;

    /** Get full metadata for a specific image by filename. */
    getImageDetails(args: { filename: string }): Promise<unknown>;

    /** List all stored images with a brief summary of each (filename, date, description, tags). */
    listImages(args: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<unknown>;

    /** Find images taken near a geographic point. Uses EXIF GPS (or channel-supplied location). Photos without GPS are excluded. Pass lat, lon, and optional radius_km (default 5). */
    nearImages(args: { lat: string; lon: string; radius_km?: string }): Promise<unknown>;
  };
  ingest: {
    /** Ingest text content ALREADY FETCHED from an external system (a Drive document, a Notion page, any integration source) into the user's document knowledge base, making it searchable via document search. Not for web pages or file uploads — those have their own ingestion paths. Re-ingesting the same uri replaces the stored version, so it is also how an updated source document is refreshed. */
    document(args: { content: string; uri: string; title: string; sourceKind: string; sourceModifiedAt?: string; ownerEmail?: string; publishedByDomain?: string }): Promise<unknown>;

    /** Report which version of an EXTERNAL document (previously ingested from an integration source like Drive or Notion) is currently held, by its source uri. Returns exists=false if never ingested; otherwise the stored title and the source's own last-modified timestamp at ingestion (sourceModifiedAt). Compare that against the live source to decide whether re-ingestion is needed. */
    status(args: { uri: string }): Promise<unknown>;
  };
  kg: {
    /** The PLAIN-ENGLISH path to the knowledge graph — third choice in the query rule (saved view → `kg_query` → this); prefer it when you would rather not author Cypher, or when a question is easier to state than to express. Plain-English question in → {"rows": [...], "warnings": [...]} (plus an optional `note` — a short caveat about THIS result, e.g. "this is an EXACT count, do not approximate"). Non-empty `warnings` means a backing source failed or truncated, so few/zero rows then means "source unavailable", not "no data"; `warnings` never carries query-shape feedback (a valid query matching nothing = 0 rows, empty warnings). A per-user-scoped Cypher query is generated DETERMINISTICALLY (strong model, temp 0) and run — this takes SECONDS, vs well under a second for `kg_query` with Cypher you write yourself. Prefer `kg_query` when you already know the query shape or latency matters (an app, a tight loop); this tool gets industry filters, multi-hop joins ("works WITH X" = colleagues at the same employer), counts, group-by, negation and disjunction right, which hand-written Cypher often does not. Pass the question FAITHFULLY — do NOT pre-narrow or reinterpret it (keep "works with X" as colleagues; "companies" as all, not just emailed ones), and for the user's OWN data keep it FIRST PERSON ("my todos", not "<owner>'s todos") — it is auto-scoped to you, so substituting the owner's name hunts for a link self-scoped entities don't have and comes back empty. A LOW or ZERO count is frequently the CORRECT answer — report it as-is; do NOT "rescue" a small result with fuzzy name-matching or alternate identifiers (email/id is the identity key; that manufactures false matches). Pass `callerModel` = your own model name/family; a FRONTIER model is told to write the Cypher itself with `kg_query`. */
    ask(args: { question: string; callerModel?: string }): Promise<{ rows: Array<Record<string, unknown>>; warnings: Array<string>; freshness?: Array<{ producer?: string; source?: string; observedAt?: string; keys?: number }>; hint?: string; cost?: { ms?: number; apiCalls?: number; llmCalls?: number } }>;

    /** Explore an entity's connections within N hops. From an entity id, walks outward and returns reachable entities { id, label, name, hops, relPath } ordered by distance — navigate from something you have instead of guessing labels. Good for fuzzy multi-hop (bill → biller → people who work there → match a name). `hops` defaults to 1 (max 3); `relTypes` (CSV) limits the edges followed. Only nodes connected to YOUR data come back. */
    neighbors(args: { id: string; hops?: number; relTypes?: string; limit?: number }): Promise<Array<{ id: string; label: string; name: string; hops: number; relPath?: Array<string> }>>;

    /** Run a raw read-only Cypher query against the user's knowledge graph. CALL SHAPE: `await gateway.kg.query({ cypher: "MATCH ...", params: "{}" })` — a SINGLE OBJECT argument, never a positional string; `params` is a JSON string ("{}" if none). (Every model gets this wrong first try — it is an object arg, not `query("...")`.) Second choice in the query rule (saved view → this → `kg_ask`): prefer it over `kg_ask` if you can write Cypher competently — sub-second, no model hop. Call `query_guide` first for the live schema. Every MATCH must name a label (`MATCH (b:Bill)`); unlabelled `MATCH (n)`, UNION and CALL are rejected. Per-user scope is injected automatically — do not add a userId filter. Returns {"rows": [...], "warnings": [...], "cost": {...}} keyed by your RETURN columns (see kg_ask for the warnings semantics). `cost.ms` is what the call took, `apiCalls` counts realm producer fetches, `llmCalls` model calls — but embedding and vector-search calls behind a semantic anchor are NOT counted, so a semantic query can report 0 and still be slow; read `ms`. Match on the identity key (email/id), NOT names; a LOW or ZERO result is usually correct — report it, don't inflate it with fuzzy fallbacks. */
    query(args: { cypher: string; params?: string }): Promise<{ rows: Array<Record<string, unknown>>; warnings: Array<string>; freshness?: Array<{ producer?: string; source?: string; observedAt?: string; keys?: number }>; hint?: string; cost?: { ms?: number; apiCalls?: number; llmCalls?: number } }>;
  };
  lens: {
    /** Declare this lens's cache freshness policy — call once with the policy object (`{ ttlSeconds, scope, invalidateOn }`). The host caches the result for `ttlSeconds` so it isn't recomputed on every open. Emitted automatically by a program lens's `cache` declaration; not for manual use. */
    cache(args: { policy: string }): Promise<unknown>;

    /** Add entities to the current lens's focus set. Preferred: pass `ids`, an array of node id strings (e.g. `{ ids: rows.map(r => r.id) }`) — no stringifying. Call repeatedly to build the focus in stages; the lens is the union of all calls. Do it AFTER any filtering. (`items`, a JSON string of ids or row objects, is also accepted for compatibility.) */
    focus(args: { ids?: unknown[]; items?: string }): Promise<unknown>;

    /** Hand back the rendered payload for this lens — call once with the object to display (e.g. a morning brief). Include a `kind` field naming its type (e.g. `kind: "briefing"`) so the surface knows how to render it; the rest is the content. This is how a lens shows a composed result, not just focused entities. Last call wins. */
    present(args: { content: string }): Promise<unknown>;
  };
  list: {
    /** What the user's own computer can be asked to do right now, via their Embabel Me app — things this appliance cannot do by itself: see what they are doing, search their open browser tabs, focus a tab, open a link, copy text, notify them. Call this FIRST whenever a request concerns the user's actual machine ("do I have a tab open…", "what am I looking at", "remind me on screen", "copy that"), then call do_host_verb. Never answer such a question from memory — only these verbs can see the machine. */
    hostVerbs(args: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<unknown>;
  };
  memory: {
    /** Persist a durable fact about the user — a preference, life fact, plan,             or correction — in plain language. Deduplication is automatic, so             re-saving known facts is safe. NOT for transient task state or             secrets (passwords, keys). */
    save(args: { fact: string }): Promise<unknown>;

    /** Recall PERSONAL FACTS the user has TOLD the assistant — preferences,             relationships, plans, work context — with provenance. Use at the START             of a task, or when the user refers to something as if you should already             know it.             This is NOT a data query. Anything about the user's structured records —             WHICH people or organizations, "who contacts/emails me most", rankings,             counts, ratings, bills, meetings, emails — is answered from the KNOWLEDGE             GRAPH, not here: run `query_guide` then `code_mode` (or a saved view via             `view_run`). If you are tempted to answer a who / which / how-many             question from memory, that is the WRONG tool — go to the graph instead.             An empty recall means it isn't in memory: do NOT loop the same search —             follow the guidance the empty result returns. Omit `query` to list all by confidence. */
    search(args: { query?: string; limit?: number }): Promise<unknown>;
  };
  notifications: {

    createNotification(args: { event: string; source: string; url?: string }): Promise<unknown>;

  openalex: {
    /** Find researchers by name. Call: searchAuthors({ search: 'A. Researcher', per_page: 1 }).. Name search over OpenAlex's disambiguated author records. Disambiguation is the point: a raw name string from a source record is not an identity — several people share it, and one person writes their name several ways.     searchAuthors(args: { search: string; per_page?: number; mailto?: string }): Promise<Record<string, unknown>>;

  openopus: {
    /** Free-text search across composers, works and genres.. Searches the whole catalogue with a single free-text `query` (e.g. 'beethoven symphony 5', 'chopin nocturne op 9'). Returns a `results` array ordered by relevance; each element carries a `composer` object and — for work hits — a `work` object. Composer-only hits set `work` to null, so to resolve a specific work take the FIRST result whose `work.id` is non-null.     omnisearch(args: { query: string; offset: number }): Promise<Openopus_OmnisearchResult>;

  progress: {
    /** Report how far along a long-running job is, so the user sees movement instead of silence. Call it as you go — after each batch, or at each phase — not once at the end.     report(args: { message: string }): Promise<unknown>;

  referenceDocs: {
    /** given a chunk ID, expand to surrounding chunks */
    broadenChunk(args: { chunkId: string; chunksToAdd?: number }): Promise<string>;

    /** Search documents with vector + full-text reciprocal-rank fusion. Call this FIRST with the user's complete question. Use vectorSearch, textSearch and expansion tools only if these fused results do not answer it. */
    fusedSearch(args: { query: string }): Promise<string>;

    /** Perform BM25 text search. Specify topK and similarity threshold from 0-1.  Query syntax: Plain text — type the user's question as they said it. Punctuation, URLs, file paths and code fragments are all safe: they are searched for, not interpreted, so nothing you write can fail to parse. Query operators are NOT available and will be matched literally if typed. Identifiers in the question — error codes, part numbers, ticket references — are matched exactly on your behalf, so you do not need to mark them. */
    textSearch(args: { query: string; topK: number; threshold?: number }): Promise<string>;

    /** Perform vector search. Specify topK. Ranking handles relevance — omit threshold unless you have a specific reason to floor it. */
    vectorSearch(args: { query: string; topK: number; threshold?: number }): Promise<string>;

    /** given a content element ID, expand to parent section. If the result is too large, use vectorSearch or textSearch with a more specific query instead. */
    zoomOut(args: { id: string }): Promise<string>;

  repository: {
    /** Create MANY entries of one type in a single call. Use this instead of repeated create_entry whenever you hold a set of records — importing a file, ingesting a export — because each call is a round-trip and thousands of them are slow and leave a partial import if one fails. Pass `rows` as an array of objects with the same field names create_entry takes. Every row is validated before any row is written, so a bad row means nothing is created. Writes are idempotent for types with an identity field, so re-running after a failure converges rather than duplicating. Relations are not supported here — use create_entry for entries that need explicit edges. */
    createEntries(args: { type: string; rows: unknown[] }): Promise<string>;

    /** Create entry. Call describe first to learn field names. Optional `relations` array adds outbound edges to other entries: `[{predicate: 'OF', to: {type: 'Movie', imdbId: 'tt...'}}]` — `to.type` names the target type, all other `to.*` fields are key properties used to find the target. The target must already exist in this world; the create is refused if it doesn't. */
    createEntry(args: { type: string; data: Record<string, unknown>; relations?: unknown[] }): Promise<string>;

    /** Delete entry by ID. */
    deleteEntry(args: { type: string; id: string }): Promise<string>;

    /** Show type schema. */
    describe(args: { type: string }): Promise<string>;

    /** Data repository for world types like todos. Pass what you want to do in 'request'. Available types: Todo, CorporateEntity, InstitutionProfile, ResearchTopic, ResearchRequest, ResearchResult, ResearchCompleted, ResearcherProfile, github.pr_review_request, github.mention, github.assignment, github.pull_request_opened, github.issue_opened, Portfolio, Agency, ProcurementGround, ProcurementCategory, Electorate, Grant, BannedPerson, Movie, StreamingService, UserStreamingSubscription, MovieTasteSummary, MovieRating, MovieReview, MusicalWork, MusicalRecording, MusicalTasteSummary, MusicalWorkRating */
    repository(args: { request: string }): Promise<string>;

    /** Update entry. Call describe first to learn field names. */
    updateEntry(args: { type: string; id: string; data: Record<string, unknown> }): Promise<string>;
  };
  save: {
    /** Save a diagram (Mermaid, graphviz, plantuml, or SVG) and return the URL to view it. Call this directly whenever the user asks for a flowchart, sequence diagram, class diagram, mindmap, or any other diagram — DO NOT write the diagram source inline as text in your reply; ALWAYS call this tool so the diagram is rendered. After calling, share the returned `/diagrams/{name}` URL with the user. For Mermaid (default and preferred) use a `.mmd` filename. */
    diagram(args: { name: string; content: string }): Promise<unknown>;
  };
  share: {
    /** Share one of the user's OWN ingested documents with another user of this installation, giving them read/search visibility of it (they cannot edit, re-share or delete it). Only the document's owner can share it. */
    document(args: { uri: string; withUser: string }): Promise<unknown>;
  };
  sql: {
    /** Run a read-only SELECT against a realm-declared SQL datasource. Args: datasource (name), query (SELECT with :named params), params (JSON object string). Returns a JSON array of row objects — an empty array means the SELECT matched no rows. If the datasource is unknown or unavailable you get an error instead, so `[]` reliably means "no rows", never "source down". */
    query(args: { datasource: string; query: string; params?: string }): Promise<unknown>;

    /** Run a write (UPDATE/INSERT/DELETE) against a realm-declared SQL datasource. Args: datasource, statement (with :named params; scope to the node by :id and assert :version for optimistic locking), params (JSON object string). Returns {"affected":n}; affected=0 means a version conflict / no match. SELECT is refused (use sql_query). */
    update(args: { datasource: string; statement: string; params?: string }): Promise<unknown>;
  };
  suggest: {
    /** Suggest capabilities this world could add: realms available to install (from the directory, minus what is already aboard), API keys that would unlock inert integrations, and structural gaps such as no documents ingested. Use when the user asks what they could add, configure, or unlock. Grounded in live world state — report it faithfully, never pad it. */
    capabilities(args: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<unknown>;
  };
  unshare: {
    /** Revoke another user's access to one of the user's OWN shared documents. Only the document's owner can revoke access. */
    document(args: { uri: string; withUser: string }): Promise<unknown>;
  };
  view: {
    /** Run one of the world's SAVED VIEWS by name and get its rows back as JSON. CALL WITH NO ARGUMENTS to LIST every view — its name, what it answers, and its parameters. Do that FIRST for any question about this world: a view that already answers the question is one call, and it encodes joins and exclusions that are easy to get wrong by hand. COST, in order — a MATERIALISED view answers from cache; a regular view and your own `kg.query` Cypher run the same engine, so they cost the same to execute and the view wins only on being correct and already written; `kg.ask` adds an LLM hop on top. A view is not automatically cheap in absolute terms: one whose rows come from a generative or fetched edge spends model and API calls to produce them. Every result reports `cost` — `ms` is what the call took, measured the same way on `view_run`, `kg.query` and `kg.ask`, so the three are directly comparable. `apiCalls` counts realm producer fetches and `llmCalls` model calls, but embedding and vector-search calls behind a semantic anchor are counted by NEITHER — a semantic query can report 0 and still be slow, so read `ms`. Pass parameters as a JSON object matching the view's declared params; omit it (or any key) to use the declared defaults. Unknown or uncoercible parameters fail with a message naming the declared ones — fix and retry. Returns {"rows": [...], "warnings": [...], "cost": {...}}. warnings is usually empty; when non-empty a backing source failed or truncated, so few/zero rows means "source unavailable", not "no data". rows are the view's OWN projection (its RETURN columns). Raw cypher instead returns {alias: value} per RETURN alias — `MATCH (x:<view>) RETURN x` yields the hydrated node's stored properties, not this projection. */
    run(args: { name?: string; params?: string }): Promise<{ rows: Array<Record<string, unknown>>; warnings: Array<string>; freshness?: Array<{ producer?: string; source?: string; observedAt?: string; keys?: number }>; hint?: string; cost?: { ms?: number; apiCalls?: number; llmCalls?: number } }>;
  };
  webhooks: {
    /** Configure an action for a webhook source. Describe what should happen when webhooks arrive from this source and the system will compile an action that runs automatically on subsequent webhooks. Any queued events are processed immediately after compilation. */
    compileWebhookAction(args: { source: string; description: string; tools: string }): Promise<unknown>;

    /** List webhook sources that have received events. Shows both configured (have an action) and queued (awaiting configuration) sources. Also shows the webhook URL pattern for registering new webhooks. */
    listWebhookSources(args: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<unknown>;

    /** Suggest useful webhooks the user could set up based on their installed APIs, MCP servers, channels, and skills. Explains what each webhook would do and how to register it with the external service. */
    suggestWebhooks(args: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<unknown>;
  };
  wikidata: {
    /** Run a SPARQL query against Wikidata. Call: sparqlQuery({ query: '...', format: 'json' }).. Returns JSON under `results.bindings[]`, each binding a map of var -> { value }. The organization-by-domain query filters on P856 (official website) so it returns at most the one entity whose site matches the domain. */
    sparqlQuery(args: { query: string; format: string }): Promise<{ results?: { bindings?: Array<Record<string, { value?: string }>> } }>;
  };
  wikipedia: {
    /** Get the lead-section summary of a Wikipedia page. Returns a clean plain-text summary of the page (typically the lead section) plus its display title, short description, and canonical URL. Pass the exact title returned by search. */
    getSummary(args: { title: string }): Promise<Wikipedia_PageSummary>;

    /** Search Wikipedia. Call: search({ q: '...', limit: 10 }). The query field is named `q`, not `query`.. Search Wikipedia for the query. Returns matching pages with title, short description, and an HTML-highlighted excerpt. Follow up with getSummary(title) to read the lead-section content of any result. The query string MUST be passed as `q` (single letter). */
    search(args: { q: string; limit?: number }): Promise<Wikipedia_SearchResponse>;

    /** Search Wikipedia and return each candidate's plain-text summary + Wikidata id in ONE call.. MediaWiki Action API search that, unlike `search`, returns for each candidate the plain-text lead `extract`, the canonical `fullurl`, and the Wikidata id (`pageprops.wikibase_item`) — everything needed to disambiguate a person to the right article. Backs the WikipediaArticle virtual-cypher join. MUST be called with `formatversion=2` so `query.pages` is an ARRAY (not an object map). */
    searchSummaries(args: { action: string; generator: string; gsrsearch: string; gsrlimit?: number; prop?: string; exintro?: number; explaintext?: number; inprop?: string; ppprop?: string; format?: string; formatversion?: number }): Promise<{ query?: { pages?: Array<{ pageid?: number; title?: string; extract?: string; fullurl?: string; pageprops?: { wikibase_item?: string } }> } }>;
  };
  world: {
    /** Research a topic in depth — gather information from web search, arXiv, and Wikipedia, then return structured findings with source URLs. Use when the user asks to research, investigate, look into, or do a deep-dive on a subject. Does NOT save a document; the user must ask explicitly for that. */
    researchTopic(args: { content: string; timestamp: string }): Promise<unknown>;

    /** Show world status: loaded skills, APIs, and world name. Only call this when the user explicitly asks about the world, what's installed, or what tools are available. Do NOT call this proactively or as a first step. */
    status(args: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<unknown>;
  };

  /** Send a permanent message to the user. Use this to report results, share links (e.g., PR URLs), or inform the user of important outcomes. Unlike progress, this creates a visible chat message. */
  communicate(args: { message: string }): Promise<unknown>;

  /** Send the user a durable notification. Background-safe: use this from an event handler to tell the user something happened. Declare the URGENCY only — the user's routing config decides which channels (inbox, Telegram, SMS, …) it actually reaches; never name a channel here. */
  notify(args: { message: string; urgency?: string; source?: string; url?: string }): Promise<unknown>;

  /** Report progress to the user. Call this during long-running work to show what you're doing. */
  progress(args: { status: string }): Promise<unknown>;
}

// The public type of the `gateway` global. Named to match validate-globals.d.ts's
// `import { GatewayContext }` — without this alias, that import resolves to nothing and, under
// tsconfig `skipLibCheck: true`, `gateway` silently degrades to `any`, so a hallucinated
// `gateway.<ns>.<method>()` type-checks clean and a broken handler saves (false success).
export type GatewayContext = WorldTools;
